name: Wendy Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a cold-heading line that forms bolt heads from wire. My two-year technical diploma covered die settings, and I can hear when a head starts forming off-centre. I like a clean first bolt; clearing tangled wire after a jam is the slow, noisy part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular hours at a pharmacy counter. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a senior operator and there are some similar metal shops nearby. I use AI now and then for long machine notes, only after the fitter has checked them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the fastener crew a little AI may tidy the order list, but a bolt head still needs a gauge. We should keep checking the first piece after each die change. That is how we stop a bad run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the cold-heading line, earn about the usual operator rate, and have four months of expenses saved. My partner has steady hours at a pharmacy counter; we have two school-age children and a mortgage. Some similar metal shops are nearby. The household feels stable at present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the bolt-head dies and checking the first pieces with a gauge. I use AI now and then to summarise long machine notes after the fitter checks them, and I'll keep comparing each summary with the actual log. I'll put a new amount from each full payday into our repair reserve after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The work is familiar, and our wages cover the house. I would still watch a tool before trusting its numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the first-piece gauge catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bolt came out with a shallow head that looked fine in the overhead photograph. I measured the first piece and stopped the reel before a full carton was made. A shallow bolt head can fail when somebody tightens it on a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pharmacy wage and mine cover the mortgage, meals and school buses. Four months saved gives us space if one of us misses work. We have a leaky bathroom tap, so new reserve money would go there before anything fancy.

say: An **order list** cannot prove bolt heads meet the gauge.
The crew should keep **first-piece checks** after die changes.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and two regular wages cover the mortgage.
Some **nearby metal shops** offer a fallback if paid work changes.
do: **Keep** gauging first bolt heads after each die change.
**Add** new money from full wages to the repair reserve after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household income.
S0.quote: A shallow bolt head can fail when somebody tightens it on a machine.
fieldNote: Wendy uses AI **occasionally** for checked summaries, while relying on a physical gauge for production quality.
Her **four-month reserve** and steady second wage support calm, with new pay funding future tap repairs.

steps.text: Keep gauging first bolt heads after die changes
Save new money from full wages into repair reserve after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may plan fastener orders before robots can move heavy reels. If a new inspection camera is offered, I would want to see it catch a known bad bolt before anyone removes the gauge check. A quicker bolt-inspection report is not the same as a sound part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My technical diploma and years on the line help me learn controls, but I do not volunteer for every new screen. Management might combine two heading shifts if the camera speeds checks, which could cut my paid hours. Four months saved helps, yet the mortgage still needs pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the lead engineer for a paid trial with a trainer on a guarded machine and a written roster comparison. If a real trial is offered, I'll practise the camera reject and safe stop on test bolts. I'll also check the actual base hours before arranging the children's pickup; if they are cut, I'll look at posted local metal jobs with enough regular pay and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible shorter roster, but I can inspect the trial results. I want the wage sheet beside the camera report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feed a bolt with a shallow head through the camera and watch whether it rejects it. Then I'd isolate the line before the trainer has me clear a jam. I would not do that first run on a live customer order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a local job need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local opening needs a posted base rate and shift times. I would compare them with our mortgage and school run, not count overtime. If a posting falls short, I keep the current shift while I look.

say: **AI planning** may reach orders before robots move bolt reels.
A **camera trial** must catch bad heads before replacing gauges.
think: A merged **heading roster** could reduce my paid hours.
Four months saved helps, but the **mortgage** needs regular wages.
do: **Request** paid guarded camera practice and written roster comparison.
**Check** base hours before changing school pickup.
**Search** posted safe local metal work if hours cut and pay and shifts fit.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour cuts with a useful trial to inspect.
S1.quote: A quicker bolt-inspection report is not the same as a sound part.
fieldNote: She accepts **new controls** after a known bad bolt proves the camera and a paid guarded trainer place is offered.
Her **job search** depends on actual base-hour cuts and posted local pay and school-compatible shifts.

steps.text: Practise camera rejects if paid guarded trainer-led trial offered
Compare written base roster before changing school pickup
Search posted safe local metal jobs if hours cut, pay and school shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI could plan fastener orders by 2028, while capable robots around 2031 could run the heading line. I would ask for a written staffing plan and the paid posts left. We should not build a family budget from a machine brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when physical robots arrive. I expect the plant could cut much of the heading crew, perhaps my lead shift too. Four months saved and a pharmacy wage could cover a search, but not a long mortgage gap. I have been awake wondering which metal shop would still hire people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask management now for written notice and any paid quality posts. If an offered funded paid-time course in guarded bolt testing has a trainer and practical seat, I'll enrol. If my hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local production jobs only when base wages and school shifts work; after qualifying, I'll apply separately for posted local testing roles under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the size of a possible crew cut. I can compare vacancies, but a four-month reserve has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should bolt-testing training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course should make me reject a shallow head, test a stripped thread and stop a jammed reel while supervised. I would not learn the safe stop on a screen alone. Paid practice matters if I am expected to sign a batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a fallback vacancy real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production fallback must actually be posted near us and show regular pay and safe duties. I would compare its shift with the school pickup and the pharmacy rota. A bolt-testing job title without a posted base rate is no offer.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before robots head bolts around 2031.
Management should publish **paid staffing plans** before the line changes.
think: At **48**, a big crew cut may reach my lead shift.
Four months saved and **pharmacy wages** cannot bridge a long gap.
do: **Ask** management for written notice and paid quality roles.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded bolt testing if a practical seat opens.
**Apply** to posted safe local production or qualified testing if cuts and pay permit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major crew loss and sleepless job worries.
S2.quote: A bolt-testing job title without a posted base rate is no offer.
fieldNote: Her **technical skill** gives a path toward quality work, but only if real paid places and vacancies appear.
The **production fallback** and qualified testing search both require posted safe local duties, sufficient base pay and family shifts.

steps.text: Ask management for written robot notice and paid quality posts
Enrol in bolt testing if funded paid guarded trainer seat offered
Apply to posted safe local production if hours cut, base pay and school shifts fit
Apply to posted safe local testing if qualified, hours cut, pay and school shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan bolts in 2031, with capable robots heading them around 2034. Five years is long enough to train a quality checker while the plant still needs our work. I would ask for a real paid seat and a posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots do the physical line work. My diploma helps with measurements, but whether another plant hires me depends on actual openings. Full pay could build more savings, and the pharmacy wage gives some help. The mortgage still needs a dependable amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll add new money from each full-pay month to our reserve after bills. I'll ask the plant for a recognized inspection certificate with covered fees, paid release and guarded practical testing. If a seat is offered, I'll take it; after qualifying, if heading hours shrink, I'll apply to posted safe local quality roles only where base pay and school hours cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later hours, with enough time to check each condition. I would rather know the rate before I make a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quality exam require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam should include a bolt with a shallow head and one with a damaged thread. I'd measure both and isolate the heading machine before signing a rejected batch. A trainer must watch that practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a nearby job still fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the base rate and shift start in a real posting. A bolt-quality job across town might look close, but a dawn shift could leave both of us unable to take the children to school. The offer has to fit the household.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before robots head bolts around 2034.
Five years allows **paid inspection training** if an actual seat and job appear.
think: At **51**, my diploma may help with quality tests.
Our **four-month reserve** could grow if full wages continue.
do: **Save** new money from full pay after bills.
**Take** funded paid guarded inspection certificate if offered.

feel: **Anxious** about future wages with time to verify terms.
S3.quote: A bolt-quality job across town might look close, but a dawn shift could leave both of us unable to take the children to school.
fieldNote: Her **new savings** come from full pay months, while the certificate requires covered fees, paid release and supervised practice.
The **quality application** follows qualification and cut hours, with an actual safe local post and sufficient base pay and school fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan fastener orders by 2036 and capable robots run the heading machines around 2039. A decade lets us see which paid roles actually remain. I would not tell the younger crew that a course name is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but the mortgage could still be there. Four months saved today gives us room to choose, while typical pay and some local plants let me prepare if work remains steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the heading line and pay extra mortgage principal from newly earned full-wage months after bills. I'll ask the local equipment supplier for written terms of its die-maintenance apprenticeship. If it offers a funded paid seat with a trainer and guarded practice, I'll take it; after qualifying, if my line hours fall, I'll apply only to posted safe local maintenance jobs whose base pay and travel work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant line change, with current wages still coming in. I can check a real training place without leaving a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to fit a worn die, isolate a reel and gauge a test bolt with the trainer beside me. I would ask who pays for that practice and whether the place is actually available. A die-maintenance sales visit is not a paid course seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would travel affect a maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A maintenance posting needs a base rate, site and normal travel days in writing. If the route clashes with school pickup or costs too much in fuel, I would keep the present shift while searching. I can wait for a viable opening.

A decade gives time to inspect **real paid roles**.
think: At **56**, I may still need a mortgage wage.
Four months saved and **some nearby shops** offer choices if pay holds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut our heading line before I have another paid role. A written staffing plan, a funded paid practical place and posted safe local work at enough base pay would help. I would check its shift with my partner's pharmacy hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gauges the first bolt after a robot changes the heading die. A carton of neat bolts can hide a bad head in every row.

headlineQuote: A carton of neat bolts can hide a bad head in every row.
portrait: **Wendy**, 43, is a senior cold-heading lead with a two-year technical diploma and strong die-setting skill.
She and her pharmacy-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with four months saved and typical pay.
Her **centre outlook** favours measured trials; she uses AI occasionally after a fitter verifies the notes.
Fast robots make her **alarmed** about a major crew cut, while paid practical learning and posted local roles offer options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable heading robots around 2031 and cut paid line work.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, funded paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient base pay would help.
